title: 335 S Broadway, De Pere, Wisconsin

movements.text: You are standing on South Broadway in De Pere, Wisconsin, in a tract that sits between two rivers. The Fox River and the East River frame the surrounding landscape, connected by the Fox River Navigational System canal and the still water of De Pere Lock. Bower Creek runs somewhere in the near distance, and Scray Hill marks the landform at the edge of the search radius. The address places you on a commercial corridor with a residential neighborhood close behind it, in a tract of just over seven thousand people.

About one in ten of the tract's housing units predate 1940 — roughly 350 structures that were already standing before the Second World War. These are the oldest bones of the neighborhood. A modest wave of construction followed in the 1940s and 1950s, adding fewer than 300 more units across two decades. The pace quickened in the 1960s and 1970s, when about 770 units went up — more than a quarter of the eventual total built in just those twenty years. The 1980s sustained that momentum with nearly 490 units, pushing the tract's median build year toward the late twentieth century. The largest single surge came between 2000 and 2009, when more than 850 units were added — nearly a quarter of all housing that exists here today. Since 2010, construction has continued at a slower rate, with about 360 more units added through 2020 and after.

movements.text: The tract holds about 3,400 occupied households. Owners outnumber renters by nearly two to one — roughly six in ten households own their homes. The median age of residents is 42, a few years above what is typical in many urban Wisconsin tracts. Most of this place drives away each morning; the commute data records no transit or bicycle trips at all, and walking accounts for fewer than one percent of workers. About 13 percent work from home. The population of just over 7,300 in a land area of roughly 19 square kilometers yields a moderate density — not dense by city standards, but not sparse either.

Eight properties within roughly 600 meters of 335 S Broadway appear on the National Register of Historic Places, and their listing dates span three decades. The De Pere Lock and Dam Historic District was listed in 1993 — the oldest listing in the immediate record. The South Broadway Historic District followed in 2010, named directly for the corridor you are standing on. Individual buildings cluster tightly: the Baeten, John, Store was listed in 2014; the Heyrman, Henry and Mary, House and the Gutknecht, Edwin and Jennie, House both in 2015, as did Nicolet High School. The Steckart and Falck Double Block was listed in 2011. Most recently, the Krause, Julius, Store Building entered the register in 2023. That's a dense concentration of named history within a five-minute walk.

Walking north from the address, you pass through the footprint of the South Broadway Historic District, where commercial storefronts give way to municipal anchors. De Pere City Hall and the De Pere Branch Brown County Library sit within the walkable radius, along with a post office. Several parks are reachable on foot — Legion Park, Voyageur Park, Bicentennial Park, and others — many equipped with sports pitches and playgrounds. The Fox River edge, with its lock and navigational infrastructure, furnishes the waterfront.

The Broadway corridor itself shows a layered street life. Restaurants and cafes are threaded through the blocks: Savour on Broadway, Café on Broadway, Luna Coffee Roasters, Black Honey Hashery, Nuk's Thai Cuisine, and Phil's are all within reach, along with Great Harvest Bread Co. Performance and arts spaces appear too — Walter Theatre, Webb Theatre, and ComedyCity De Pere are all mapped within 1,200 meters. St. Norbert College's presence is registered in the data through the St. Norbert College Children's Center and the Van Dyke Gym. The street does not thin out at the edges; it simply changes register.
